title: Fix mode and re-review rules

story: Byte, our review agent, left two findings on your PR. You fix both in a two-line commit and push. A cheap check called the sniff runs first and answers within seconds: both findings fixed, and it is sure. Then Byte runs a full review anyway, five more minutes and about two more dollars, and tells you what you already knew.

In fcp this happens on every push like yours, because the sniff runs in observe mode: it gives its answer, and nobody acts on it. Switching it on would save a full review on many pushes. But if the sniff says fixed when it is not, a push reaches main without the review it needed.
hook.question: When has a cheap check earned enough trust to replace the expensive one, and how many examples does that take?

read.h: The sniff, and why it only watches
p: After Byte's first review of a PR, every new push still has open findings: the comments Byte left that nobody has fixed yet. The sniff is a very small model call (it runs on Jev, a small model from an outside company called TypeSafe, and costs about a hundredth of a cent) that gets the new diff and the open findings, and answers for each finding: fulfilled or not, with a confidence between 0 and 1. A fulfilled answer counts as sure when its confidence is at least 0.85, a setting called fulfilConfidence. When every open finding is fulfilled and sure, Byte can post one short line instead of running a full review.

In fcp the sniff runs in observe mode. It answers and its answer is stored, but the full review runs every time. That sounds wasteful, but it is the most useful data we have, because every sniff now has a partner: the full review of the same push. If the sniff said fixed and sure, and the full review flagged the same finding again, the sniff was wrong. Each stored pair looks roughly like this.

p: Two things can go wrong with a live sniff, and each gets its own number. The dangerous one is a false fulfilled: the sniff said fulfilled and sure, but the paired full review flagged the finding again. In live mode that push would have skipped a review it needed. The bar is at most 2% of sure answers.

The other number is about whether switching is worth it at all. The skip rate is the share of all-fixed pushes where the sniff was sure about every finding, so live mode would really skip the review. If it is low, the sniff is safe but saves almost nothing, and we have added a moving part for no gain. The bar is at least 40%.

read.h: Sixty out of sixty is not proof
p: Say the first week of pairs has 60 sure answers, and none of them was wrong. It is tempting to read that as a 0% error rate and switch. But think of a new restaurant with three five-star reviews: you trust it less than a place with 3,000 reviews averaging 4.8, even though 5.0 is the higher number. With few examples, luck plays a big part, and 60 clean answers fit a sniff whose true error rate is 0.5%, but also one whose rate is 5%.

A confidence interval says how far the true rate could be from the rate you saw. For rates near zero the right tool is the Wilson score interval, and we only need its upper end: the highest true rate the data still allows, at 95% confidence. We compare that upper end with the 2% bar, not the rate we saw. Zero wrong out of 60 gives an upper end of 6.0%, so the answer is not yet. With zero wrong you need about 190 sure answers before the upper end falls under 2%, and one wrong answer moves that to about 280. That is why the rule says: with too few pairs, wait another week instead of lowering the bar.

notes.text: No data at all: any rate is possible, so the bar fails safely.

read.h: The switch, and what it never skips
p: When both bars hold on live data, going live is one key in Byte's policy file: fcp's sniff.observe becomes false, and every other key stays the same. Byte reviews that PR, and the person who maintains Byte approves it.

Some pushes always get a full review, whatever the sniff says: a push that touches a sensitive path (authentication, migrations, workflows or infrastructure), a PR with any open high-severity finding, and any PR where someone comments @byte-review. After the switch, the weekly report keeps watching how often a full review re-flags a finding the sniff called fixed. If that goes over 2% in the first two weeks, observe is set back to true. The sniff stays on Jev instead of a bigger model, because its thresholds were tuned on Jev and a sniff costs about $0.0001.

notes.text: The whole change: observe goes from true to false.
Unchanged: a fulfilled answer counts as sure from 0.85.

deeper.h: Go deeper: when Byte writes the fix itself
p: There is a second rule about what happens after a review. Anyone can comment @byte-fix on a PR, and Byte writes a small fix PR into the author's branch. Picture a reviewer who asks Byte to fix two findings, the author merges the fix into their branch, and then the same reviewer approves the PR to main. The person who asked for that code approved it, which breaks our rule that the requester never approves their own agent's work. Today only a team habit prevents it.

The fix is to make it visible to GitHub. Byte adds a trailer, a Key: value line at the end of a commit message, to every fix commit: Requested-by: followed by the login Byte's gate already checked when it accepted the command, never text from the model. The independent-approval check on main then reads the Requested-by trailers of Byte's fix commits, adds those people to the requester set, and accepts only an approval that is newer than the last fix commit and comes from someone outside that set. Green checks need no new work: merging the fix changes the PR's head, so the required checks run again and the main ruleset drops older approvals. No new workflow runs on the fix PR itself, because Security's sign-off on fix mode depends on none running there.

lab.title: Decide when the sniff may go live
lab.goal: Compute the Wilson upper bound, run the go-live decision on three weeks of observe-mode pairs, and find how many examples the 2% bar needs.

guess.q: In its first week, the sniff gave 60 sure 'fulfilled' answers and none was wrong. With a bar of at most 2% false fulfilled, measured by the Wilson upper bound, can it go live?

options.why: 0% is what you saw. With only 60 examples the true rate could still be up to 6%.

options.text: No: the upper bound is about 6%, so it waits for more pairs
options.why: With zero wrong answers it takes about 190 sure answers before the upper bound drops under 2%.

options.text: No: one week of data is never enough, whatever the numbers
options.why: Time is not the rule; the number of pairs is. A busy week with 300 good pairs would be enough.

check.q: Observe mode in fcp has produced 60 sure 'fulfilled' answers, none of them wrong. What should happen?

options.text: Go live: 0% is far under the 2% bar
options.why: 0% is the rate you saw. The Wilson upper bound for 0 of 60 is about 6%, above the bar.

options.text: Lower the bar to 6% for the first month
options.why: The rule is the opposite: with too few pairs, wait rather than lower the bar.

options.text: Wait for more pairs: with no wrong answers it takes about 190 before the bound drops under 2%
options.why: More examples narrow the interval. Time costs nothing here, because observe mode keeps the full review running.

check.q: What does a false fulfilled mean?

options.text: The sniff said fulfilled and sure, and the paired full review flagged the same finding again
options.why: That is a push live mode would have let through without the review it needed.

options.text: The sniff said not fulfilled, but the developer had fixed the finding
options.why: That mistake only costs an extra full review, which is what happens today anyway.

options.text: The full review found a new problem that the sniff did not mention
options.why: The sniff only judges the open findings. New problems in changed code are a different question.

check.q: The sniff is live in fcp. A push touches a migration, and the sniff says every open finding is fulfilled and sure. What happens?

options.text: Byte posts the short sniff line and skips the review
options.why: Sensitive paths, migrations among them, always get a full review.

options.text: A full review runs, because the push touches a sensitive path
options.why: The sniff only replaces reviews of ordinary pushes. Authentication, migrations, workflows and infrastructure always get the full review.

options.text: The sniff runs again at a higher confidence
options.why: There is no second sniff. The path decides that the full review runs.

p: Byte's sniff data lives on its telemetry branch, in data/sniffs.jsonl and data/sniff-pairs.jsonl, shown on the dashboard's sniff page. Read fcp's rows with Nave, check both bars on live data (false fulfilled at most 2% by the Wilson upper bound, skip rate at least 40%), then open the one-line PR that sets fcp's sniff.observe to false in config/repositories.json. Nothing else changes: SENSITIVE_PATH pushes and any open high finding still get a full review, @byte-review still forces one, and the sniff stays on jev-1.13.0. Watch the weekly harvest's re-flag rate for two weeks and set observe back to true if it goes over 2%.

The fix-mode rule changes src/fix-render.ts in Byte (a Requested-by trailer on fix commits and a Requested-by line in the fix PR body, from the gate-validated login), extends the independent-approval check on fcp main to read those trailers, updates SECURITY.md residuals 1 and 5, and sends the fix-PR merge rate from data/fix-fates.jsonl to Grafana as byte_fix_prs_total{state} through the nightly metrics job.

tickets.why: Taking the sniff out of observe mode in fcp, once both bars hold.
Byte's fix commits carry Requested-by, and the check on main enforces an independent, newer approval.

words.plain: A very cheap model call on each new push that says, per open finding, whether it was fixed, with a confidence.
The sniff answers and its answer is stored, but the full review still runs, so every answer can be checked.
The sniff said fixed and sure, but the full review flagged the same finding again.
The share of all-fixed pushes on which a live sniff would really skip the full review.
The highest true rate your data still allows, at 95% confidence. With few examples it stays high.
A Key: value line at the end of a commit message, such as Requested-by: omer, that tools can read.

review.q: From memory: the two bars for taking the sniff live, and why each one exists.
review.a: False fulfilled at most 2% (by the Wilson upper bound), so a skipped review is rarely one that was needed; skip rate at least 40%, so switching saves enough to be worth it.

review.q: A teammate says: 'Zero mistakes in 100 answers, ship it.' What do you answer, with numbers?
review.a: Zero of 100 still allows a true rate of about 3.7% at 95% confidence. With zero mistakes we need about 190 sure answers before the upper bound is under 2%, so we wait, which costs nothing because the full review still runs.

review.q: Which pushes always get a full review, even with the sniff live?
review.a: Pushes that touch sensitive paths (authentication, migrations, workflows, infrastructure), PRs with an open high-severity finding, and PRs where someone comments @byte-review.

remember: Let a cheap check watch beside the expensive one, and switch only when the Wilson upper bound of its mistakes is under the bar, not when the mistakes you saw happen to be zero.
